'''''Oenanthe pimpinelloides''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Apiaceae]] known by the common name '''corky-fruited water-dropwort'''. It is a plant of tall, lightly grazed or infrequently mown [[grassland]] and coastal meadows in Europe and neighbouring parts of Asia and North Africa.
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides flowers.jpg|thumb|The outer flowers have enlarged "radiating" petals.]]

==Description==
Corky-fruited water-dropwort is a hairless, upright [[Perennial plant|perennial]] with a solid, strongly grooved stem measuring up to 100 cm in height and 0.5 cm in diameter. The roots contain ovoid tubers a short distance from the base of the stem. The lanceolate to ovate lower leaves are twice pinnate with broad, toothed, [[cuneate leaf|cuneate]] segments 55 mm long and have a petiole up to 10 cm long. The petiole may exude sparse white latex when pierced.<ref>Poland J, Clements EJ. 2009. ''Vegetative Key to the British Flora''. BSBI.</ref> The upper leaves are once- or twice-pinnate, and the blade is at least the same length as the [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]; the linear, entire lobes are 10–30 mm long.<ref name = "Tutin">Tutin TG. 1980. ''Umbellifers of the British Isles''. BSBI Handbook No. 2. {{ISBN|0-9-0115802-X}}</ref>

The main [[umbels]] each have of 6–15 smooth rays, 1–2 cm long, which thicken after flowering. Below these rays is a whorl of up to 5 small linear-lanceolate bracts. The [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] of the secondary umbels (umbellules) are longer than the rays and also thicken after flowering, producing fruiting heads that are distinctively flat-topped. Each umblellule is subtended by 12-20 small, linear bracteoles.

It flowers from June to August in the UK.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref> The terminal umbels have both male-only and bisexual flowers, while the lateral umbels produce only male flowers. The non-fruiting male-only flowers are on longer stalks (pedicels) than the bisexual ones. Each tiny flower has 5 pointed, green sepals and 5 white petals, the outermost of which are slightly larger (a phenomenon known as "radiating"). There are 5 stamens, and 2 styles which project from the bulbous centre of the flower (the stylopodium). The stylopodium is the organ which secretes nectar onto its surface, attracting unspecialised species of pollinating insect, such as flies. The fruit is a schizocarp: a hard capsule that splits into two one-seeded mericarps as it matures. Each schizocarp is 3-3.5 mm long, with a prominent ridge on each mericarp. Like the rays and the peduncles, the individual pedicels also thicken after flowering.<ref name = "Tutin"/><ref name="Sell3" />
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides stem.jpg|thumb|The lower part of the stem is often tinged purple]]
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides fruits.jpg|thumb|A fruiting umbel, showing the characteristic flat top and the long pedicels where male flowers have faded.]]

==Identification==
Unlike other species in the genus, ''Oenanthe pimpinelloides'' has ovoid to globose root tubers (‘potatoes’) that are situated some distance from the base of the stem. [[Oenanthe silaifolia|Narrow-leaved water-dropwort]] may also have tubers of this shape (the only other species displaying such a character), but in contrast to ''O. pimpinelloides'', these are held close to the base of the plant.<ref>Southam M. 1996. Recurring problems in ''Oenanthe''. ''BSBI News'' 71: 22 – 24.</ref> However, on the grounds of conservation and wildlife law, the plant should not be uprooted to examine this character for identification purposes; different morphological features and habitat context should be looked at instead.<ref>Rose F, Walls RM. ''Oenanthe'', fined leaved species. In: Rich TCG, Jermy AC. 1998. ''Plant Crib''. BSBI.</ref>

Amongst the British species, corky-fruited water-dropwort is distinctive because it tends to grow in dry habitats and has flat-topped umbels. The bracts distinguish it from [[Oenanthe silaifolia|narrow-leaved water-dropwort]], which has similarly fine foliage.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

''O. pimpinelloides'' has been frequently confused with the very similar ''O. incrassans'' in southeast Europe, which is sometimes treated as a subspecies.<ref>Foley MJY, Southam MJ. 2007. ''Oenanthe incrassans'' Bory & Chaub. (Apiaceae), a distinctive plant of the Aegean region. ''Candollea'' 62(2). ISSN: 0373-2967.</ref><ref>Güner ED. 2016. ''Oenanthe incrassans'': an enigmatic species from Turkey and its comparison with ''Oenanthe pimpinelloides'' (Apiaceae). ''Phytokeys'' 62: 101 – 111. doi: 10.3897/phytokeys.62.8106</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides foliage.jpg|thumb|The upper leaves have narrow, linear segments]]

==Taxonomy and nomenclature==
The scientific name for corky-fruited water-dropwort was coined by [[Peter Artedi]], who developed the modern [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial]] classification system, and defined the species on the basis of its [[Bract|involucral]] characters.<ref name=constance>{{cite book |last1=Constance |first1=L. |title=History of the classification of Umbelliferae (Apiaceae) ''in Heywood, V. H. (ed.) The Biology and Chemistry of the Umbelliferae''|date=1971 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |pages=1–11}}</ref> However, Artedi's original ''Oenanthe pimpinelloides'' was not adequately separated from ''[[Oenanthe lachenalii|O. lachenalii]]'' and it was not until 1844 that a useful distinction between those two species was made.<ref name=Bristol />

The original (ambiguous) name was published after Artedi's death by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in [[Species Plantarum]], in 1753, and that name still stands for this species, although numerous synonyms have been proposed over the years, including ''Oenanthe globosa'' Georgi (1800), ''Oenanthe graminifolia'' Gaudin (1828), ''Oenanthe anatolica'' K. Koch (1846), and ''Phellandrium mathioli'' Bubani (1899). A full list can be found in the Synonymic Checklists of the Plants of the World.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=M. |title=Synonymic Checklists of the Vascular Plants of the World |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5371889/treatments}}</ref>

The following subspecies are currently recognised: ''O. pimpinelloides'' subsp. ''incrassans'' (Bory & Chaub.) Strid (2012), which occurs only in [[Greece]];<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Oenanthe pimpinelloides subsp. incrassans |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/7716198}}</ref> ''O. pimpinelloides'' subsp. ''callosa'' (Salzm. ex DC.) Maire, which is only in [[Morocco]];<ref>{{Cite web |title=Oenanthe pimpinelloides subsp. callosa (Salzm. ex DC.) Maire {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77251294-1 |access-date=2025-12-05 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> and ''O. pimpinelloides'' subsp. ''pimpinelloides'', which accounts for all other populations but is rarely recorded.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Oenanthe pimpinelloides subsp. pimpinelloides |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/7342779}}</ref>

There are no reported hybrids.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 22.<ref name="Tutin" />

The generic name ''[[Oenanthe (plant)|Oenanthe]]'', which comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] οίνος, "wine" and άνθος, "flower", was used in ancient times for certain Mediterranean plants and later adopted to describe this genus. The Latin [[specific epithet]] “pimpinelloides” means “resembling ''[[Pimpinella]]''”, another genus in the same family (Apiaceae). The "dropwort" part of the common name is a reference to the tubers produced amongst the roots of this and certain other species in the [[Oenanthe (plant)|genus]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wiktionary |title=dropwort |date=18 August 2024 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dropwort}}</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides old fruit.jpg|thumb|Mature fruit]]

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides sward.jpg|thumb|A corky-fruited water-dropwort meadow in Kent.]]
This is a plant of damp to dry grassland, hay meadows, old pastures and roadsides. Being more resistant to [[water stress (plants)|water stress]] than its congeners,<ref>Radutoiu D, Stan I, Costache I. 2014. ''Oenanthe pimpinelloides'' L. in the flora of Romania. ''Contribuţii Botanice''  49: 61 – 66.</ref> it is the only water-dropwort that grows in dry lowland habitats in some parts of its natural range.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref> Although it is usually described as a grassland plant, its habitat is often somewhat ruderal and tending towards scrub. In Sardinia, it has been described as a plant of [[Myrtus communis|myrtle]] scrub around Mediterranean temporary ponds,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fois |first1=M. |title=Discovering neglected vegetation in Sardinia: from knowledge to conservation |url=https://iris.unica.it/handle/11584/322971 |website=UNICA IRIS Institutional Research Information System |access-date=25 December 2022}}</ref> and in Turkey it is often found under hazel trees.<ref name="Arslan" />

Under the [[European Environment Agency|European Nature Information]] classification system EUNIS it is considered a characteristic species of "Atlantic [[Arrhenatherum elatius|false oat-grass]] meadows" (E2.211), which are restricted to the southern parts of the British Isles and western France.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EUNIS -Factsheet for Atlantic [Arrhenatherum] grasslands |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/habitats/4022 |access-date=2024-06-07 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref> This is equivalent to [[Mesotrophic grasslands in the British National Vegetation Classification system|MG1 ''Arrhenatherum elatius'']] in the [[British National Vegetation Classification|British NVC]], although it was omitted from the original description of that community.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vols. 1-5 |date=1991–2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref> False oat-grass meadows are characteristic of southern English counties such as Somerset and Hampshire, although this community is now more often found on road verges and field margins.<ref name="Bristol">{{Cite book |last=White |first=J.W. |title=The Bristol Flora |publisher=R.A. Blackwell & Partners |year=1912 |location=Bath}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=The flora of Hampshire: a continuation of the work of Alick Westrup and Phoebe Yule |date=1996 |publisher=Harley in association with the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust |isbn=978-0-946589-53-1 |editor-last=Brewis |editor-first=Anne |location=Colchester |editor-last2=Bowman |editor-first2=Paul |editor-last3=Rose |editor-first3=Francis}}</ref>

A different, but analogous, habitat for it is the EUNIS "Mediterranean tall humid grasslands" (E3.1), which are widespread throughout southern Europe as far east as the Black Sea.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EUNIS -Factsheet for Mediterranean tall humid grassland |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/habitats/161 |access-date=2024-06-07 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref>

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 7, R = 6, N = 3, and S = 0.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

Five species of insect are known to feed on corky-fruited water-dropwort in the UK. Three of these are [[fly|flies]]: ''[[Kiefferia pericarpiicola]]'' larvae produce galls on the flowers and seeds; ''[[Lasioptera]] carophila'' is a midge which also produces galls in the flowers or stems; and [[carrot fly]] can attack the roots. The remaining two species are [[Lepidoptera]]: ''[[Depressaria daucella]]'' caterpillars feed among the flowerheads, while ''[[Agonopterix yeatiana]]'' larvae roll the leaves and shoots.<ref name=PIDB>{{cite web |last1=Biological Records Centre |title=Insects and their food plants |url=http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=3625 |access-date=23 December 2022}}</ref>
[[File:Depressaria daucella Caterpillar MHNT.jpg|thumb|Larva of ''Depressaria daucella'' on a flowerhead of ''O. pimpinelloides'']]

''O. pimpinelloides'' can be a [[noxious weed]] in New Zealand on account of its vigorous, persistent growth where no natural enemies occur, potentially outcompeting native eucalypts.<ref>McKenzie H, Davenhill N, Gifford H, Hawke A. 1998. Growth of ''Eucalyptus nitens'' after application of herbicide to control parsley dropwort. ''Proceedings of the New Zealand Plant Protection Conference'' 51: 241 – 244.</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe pimpinelloides pollinator.jpg|thumb|Pollination is by unspecialised insects such as this bonking beetle, ''[[Rhagonycha fulva]]'']]

==Distribution and status==
Corky-fruited water-dropwort is widely distributed in Europe, ranging from western Ireland and southern Britain to Turkey, then into western Asia including Israel, Jordon, Lebanon, and Syria. It also extends south through France, Spain, Portugal, and Morocco.<ref>Cook CDK. 1968. ''Oenanthe''. In: Tutin ''et al.'' (eds.). ''Flora Europaea''. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2: 338-339.</ref>

The centre of the world distribution of corky-fruited water-dropwort (''Œnanthe faux boucage'') is in France, where it is most common in the south-west, and overall is classified as [[Least-concern species|"Least Concern"]]. However, it becomes scarcer ([[Vulnerable species|VU]]) inland in places like the [[Rhône-Alpes]] region and even [[Critically Endangered]] at the northern edge of its range in [[Upper Normandy]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Œnanthe faux boucage, Œnanthe faux pimpinelle |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/109893 |access-date=10 June 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref><ref name=Guillemot>{{Cite book |last=Guillemot |first=Vincent |title=Flore du Massif armoricain et ses marges |publisher=Editions Biotope |year=2023 |isbn=978-2-36662-301-7 |location=Mèze |language=fr}}</ref>

In the UK, its natural range is restricted to a few counties such as [[Somerset]], [[Dorset]], and [[Hampshire]]; where it is locally common.<ref name = "Tutin"/> However, it may be naturalized elsewhere in the country, such as in [[Cambridgeshire]]. In 2006, several plants were discovered growing around fishermen’s platforms dug into the bank of a lake at [[RAF Waterbeach]].<ref>Leslie A. 2007. Vascular Plant Records. ''Nature in Cambridgeshire'' 49: 89 – 95.</ref> The following year, about a dozen plants were found growing in a naturalized state on a lawn around a small pond at the British Antarctic Headquarters at High Cross, Cambridge.<ref>Cadbury CJ. 2010. Water dropwort ''Oenanthe'' species in Cambridgeshire. Nature in Cambridgeshire, No. 52.</ref>

A new Irish record for the species was made at [[Duncannon]] in [[County Wexford]] in 2006.<ref>Green PR. 2008. ''Oenanthe pimpinelloides'' (corky fruited water dropwort) found at Duncannon, New for County Wexford (V.C. H12). ''Irish Botanical News'' 18: p31.</ref>

==Uses==
The related species [[Oenanthe crocata|hemlock water-dropwort]] is highly poisonous, and it is often assumed that corky-fruited water-dropwort would be similarly dangerous,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Corky-fruited water-dropwort (Oenanthe pimpinelloides) wildflower |url=https://plantwild.co.uk/product/corky-fruited-water-dropwort/ |access-date=2024-06-06 |website=Plant Wild |language=en-GB}}</ref> but there is no record of it ever harming humans or livestock, and it often occurs in hay meadows and pastures without any ill effect on cattle, sheep or horses.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref><ref name="Atlas" />

[[Maud Grieve|Mrs Grieve]] described it as innocuous, and suggested that the tubers have "something the flavour of a [[Hazelnut|filbert]]"; she did not consider it to have any medicinal properties, however.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref> In Turkey it is reported to be consumed by the locals after roasting or cooking with yoghurt and [[bulgur]] wheat<ref>Ozbek K, Karabak S, Aysar N, Guzelsoy NA, Nurgal SARI, Duran RM, Tasci R, Guner B, Yucearslan H, Deniz D, Aksoy A. 2017. Biodiversity for food and nutrition project: Black Sea region studies ''ANADOLU Ege Tarımsal Araştırma Enstitüsü Dergisi'' 27(2): 17 - 25.</ref> or pickled and cooked in the winter. It is said to be used as a digestive stimulant.<ref name = Arslan>{{cite journal |last1=Arslanoglu |first1=S.F. |title=Some medicinal plants gathered from natural areas |journal=Lucrări Ştiinţifice |date=2016 |volume=59 |issue=2}}</ref>
